Lethargic

/luh-THAR-jik/ - the stress falls on THAR · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Lethargic means sluggish and lacking energy.

The flu left Amara lethargic for a week, and even lifting the kettle felt like a chore worth planning.

Worked Example

Nobody warned the new keeper about February at the reptile house: the iguanas go lethargic in the short days, draping their branches like wet towels and stirring only when the heat lamps cycle on.

Lethargic describes energy at low tide — sluggish in body, slow to stir, every action costing more than it should. It runs deeper than 'tired': a nap fixes tired, while lethargy hangs on, dragging at the whole system.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

listless: without interest or spark; the mood side of low energy

drowsy: heavy with sleep specifically

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

energetic: full of active force and stamina

peppy: bright, bouncy, and quick to move

Where it sits · how deep the energy drain runs — tired → sluggish → lethargic

tired vs. lethargic: Tired is the everyday rung, well below lethargic — a good night's sleep cures tired.

sluggish vs. lethargic: Sluggish comes closer but stops short of lethargic — sluggish slows your morning, while lethargic drags at the whole day and will not lift.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — leth-

Root — leth-: forgetfulness (Greek lethe)

Root — arg-

Root — arg-: idle, inactive (Greek argos)

Suffix — -ic

Suffix — -ic: characterized by

Put it together

Put it together: Leth- (Greek lethe, 'forgetfulness') + arg- (Greek argos, 'idle') + -ic = in a state of forgetful idleness. Greek physicians named lethargos the drowsy stupor in which patients forgot the world, and myth kept the image: Lethe was the underworld river whose water erased memory. Lethargic still carries both halves — energy gone, and the world grown dim.

Why there's no relative to spot

Why there's no relative to spot: Greek lethe ('forgetfulness') left no other common English word — even 'lethal' is a false friend, from Latin letum ('death'), not from forgetting. Lethe itself survives only as the name of the mythical river whose water washed memory away.

Strength Check

Word Choice

neutral / clinical

Lethargic is the word doctors and vets reach for: a flat, lasting energy drain, often a symptom. Use 'tired' for what sleep will fix and 'sluggish' for a slow patch; call someone lethargic when the battery itself seems drained — days of it, not hours.
